new_statements.quote: All attested Ron languages have three level tones as well as combination tones and this can therefore be posited in Proto-Ron. Tones have significant grammatical functions as well as lexical — for example making plurals or deriving verbs from nouns.
new_statements.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2003. Why reconstructing comparative Ron is so problematic. In H. Ekkehard Wolff (ed.), Topics in Chadic linguistics, 21-42. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (23-page scan, no text; the PDF's metadata: MiraScan/Acrobat Paper Capture 2005) and the page scan = printed p. 28. The image shows the heading "3.3 Tones" followed by exactly: "All attested Ron languages have three level tones as well as combination tones and this can therefore be posited in Proto-Ron. Tones have significant grammatical functions as well as lexical –for example making plurals or deriving verbs from nouns." The quote is verbatim (the only difference is dash spacing). The scanned text ( lines 297-302) matches. The whole scanned has no occurrence of stress, accent or pitch; "prosodies" appears only in §3.2 for labial/palatal consonant prosodies (p. 27-28). Surrounding…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ron (all lects, including Daffo-Butura and Bokkos) is a tone language with three level tones plus contour ('combination') tones; tone is lexically and grammatically contrastive. No source opened says anything about word stress or accent; none states a stress position and none states that stress is absent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source also notes that falling tones in Sha and Karfa arose from tone coalescence after shortening of a long internal vowel (p. 29), i.e. contour tones are partly historical.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the tone system of the Ron group as a whole (comparative paper drawing on Seibert's and Blench's wordlists), not a word-prosody description of ronn1241 specifically; word-level lexical/grammatical tone, citation forms in wordlists.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog ronn1241 'Ron' covers the Daffo-Butura, Bokkos, Monguna/Shagawu, Mbar and Mangar lects (Blench treats these as separate languages). The quoted Blench 2003 statement is made for 'all attested Ron languages', i.e. it also covers Fyer (fyer1238), Sha (shaa1241), Kulere/Richa (kule1250), Mundat and Karfa, which have their own glottocodes; the saved Bokkos dictionary is the Bokkos lect, the Seibert TOC and numerals are the Daffo lect. Mallan 2016 calls its variety 'Ron-murwi'.
